title: Hosted API surface patterns for sparse updates and tool handshake
content:
Summary:
This is a working PRD sketch proposing a lightweight, interoperable set of Hosted API patterns aimed at: 1) allowing models to emit sparse/delta updates (not just token stream), 2) supporting a robust tool-calling handshake that is versioned and resumable, and 3) giving SDKs ergonomic primitives for consuming/controlling these flows. The goal is a minimal surface that unlocks common product use cases (long-running updates, tool orchestration, structured outputs) while keeping latency and cost predictable.

Problem statement (short):
- Customers want streaming that is more structured than a raw token stream: e.g., partial JSON objects, status updates, progress checkpoints, and intermittent tool-call requests.
- Current hosted API streaming patterns force either fully synchronous tool orchestration (block until tool completes) or brittle ad-hoc encodings (embed JSON in text tokens).
- SDK ergonomics for resuming interrupted streams, backpressure, and typed parsing are inconsistent across languages.

User stories:
- As an engineer, I want the model to return progress events (percent_complete) and checkpoints (schema-validated partial output) so I can update UI without waiting for final generation.
- As a platform user, I want the model to request an external tool (search, DB write) via a standardized handshake and receive a typed response without the app developer writing custom parsers.
- As an SDK consumer, I want a simple async iterator that yields typed frames, supports resume after network blips, and exposes cost/latency metadata per frame.

Success metrics (suggested):
- Reduce app-level parsing errors from ad-hoc JSON-in-text by 90% for pilot customers.
- 10% reduction in user-observed latency for early UI updates (first-progress event emitted faster).
- Zero-severity incidents in first 3 months caused by tool-calling mismatch (versioning/handshake issues).

Non-goals:
- This doc is not trying to replace full function-calling spec implementations (e.g., complete JSON-RPC over websockets). It proposes a pragmatic subset tailored to Hosted API constraints and model runtimes.

Design principles:
- Minimal orthogonal frame types: keep the wire protocol small so existing streaming infra (SSE/HTTP/WS) can be reused.
- Explicit schemas for structured frames so SDKs can auto-validate/parsing without brittle heuristics.
- Resume/resilience: include lightweight checkpointing metadata so clients can reconnect and continue reading from a known point.
- Backward compatible: a token/text-only fallback must be supported for legacy clients.

Wire-level primitives (frames):
We propose that every stream consists of a sequence of frames. Each frame is typed and carries optional metadata. Frames are line-delimited JSON (SSE-friendly) or an equivalent binary frame in WS. Frame types:
- meta: stream-level info (stream_id, model, start_time, schema_hint) emitted once at start
- delta: continuation/partial text output (free-form) for backwards compatibility
- structured: typed payloads (id, schema_id, payload) for checkpointed JSON blobs
- progress: progress updates (percent, status, eta_ms)
- tool_call: model->platform request to invoke tool (tool_id, call_id, input_schema, input_payload, timeout_ms, auth_hint)
- tool_result: platform->model response (call_id, status, result_schema, result_payload, error)
- finalize: stream end (final schema reference, checksum, cost_summary)

Notes on structured frames:
- schema_id points to an entry in the Hosted API schema registry (short id + optional version). This lets the model/SDK negotiate a minimal shape without embedding large schema text in every frame.
- payload is always JSON. SDKs may validate against the registry before passing to the app.

Tool-calling handshake (proposal):
1) Capability advertisement: platform sends the model a set of available tools at the start (meta frame contains tools: [tool_id, version, capability_tags, auth_modes]). This is a small capability map for the model to reference.
2) tool_call frame emitted by model with call_id (UUID), tool_id, input_schema reference and encoded input_payload. Model may include intent metadata (why this tool).
3) Platform acknowledges (200-like tool_result ack) immediately when it has accepted the invocation (tool_result status: accepted, queued).
4) Platform executes the tool in the customer's environment (Dedicated/Private: runs in VPC).
5) Platform returns tool_result with final status and typed result_payload or an error code. The model may emit follow-up structured frames referencing the call_id.

Important constraints and behavioral rules: 
- tool_call frames are advisory: platform may refuse if tool unavailable, out-of-quota, or unsafe. A refusal is returned with structured reason codes. Model should degrade gracefully (fallback_policy indicated in meta).
- tool_call timeouts: the model expresses desired timeout_ms; platform enforces a configured max per-tenant. If the tool does not respond, platform returns tool_result status: timeout and the model can choose alternate behavior.
- Security: input_payload may contain references to customer data. Platform must not send secrets back to model. auth_hint on tool_call suggests how to obtain any required credentials.

SDK ergonomics (language-agnostic primitives):
High-level API should present two main flows: GeneratedStream and ToolSession.
- GeneratedStream: async iterator that yields Frame objects. Frames are typed (enum) and include metadata. Example pseudocode:
  stream = client.generate_stream(req)
  async for frame in stream:
    if frame.type == 'progress': ui.update(frame.payload)
    if frame.type == 'structured': handle_checkpoint(frame.payload)
    if frame.type == 'tool_call': await tool_session.handle_remote_call(frame)

- ToolSession: encapsulates tool execution. SDK exposes accept(call) -> ticket; ticket.resolve(result) -> sends tool_result. ToolSession handles retries, timeouts, and auth hints. The pattern aims to keep the app code small.

Resume and checkpoints: 
- Each structured frame may include checkpoint_id and offset. Clients that disconnect can reconnect with ?resume_from=checkpoint_id and the server will replay frames after that checkpoint. Keep retention window short (configurable per-tenant) to avoid indefinite state.
- For long-running flows, include occasional full-checkpoint frames (complete object) and smaller delta structured frames (patches).

Backpressure and flow control: 
- Provide a simple credits token mechanism in meta: initial_credit_count. SDKs can ACK frames when processed; server should pause generation if unacked > threshold for that connection. This prevents models from overwhelming clients, especially when tool calls are frequent.

Telemetry and observability: 
Emit structured telemetry events at these boundaries: stream_start, each_tool_call_request, tool_call_ack, tool_call_complete, stream_checkpoint_emitted, stream_finalize. Track latency and cost per-frame to make unit economics visible in Console.

Compatibility and fallback strategy: 
- Server must accept legacy clients that only read a free-form token stream: in this case the runtime will interleave text deltas and omit structured frames.
- SDKs should expose a compatibility mode which returns text-only frames for older apps.

Acceptance criteria for an initial alpha: 
- SDKs (JS + Python) implement GeneratedStream and ToolSession prototypes and pass integration tests for: tool call request/ack/result loop, resume from checkpoint, and progress frames.
- Backend implements frame encoding/decoding + per-tenant retention for checkpoints and a basic schema registry stub.
- Console shows per-stream telemetry for 50 pilot customers.

Rollout plan (phased):
1) Prototype internal-only: wire-level frames over WS and SSE, SDK prototypes, internal apps (solutions demos) use tool-call flow. (4 weeks)
2) Private beta with 10 customers: add schema registry, auth_hint flows, and telemetry. (8 weeks)
3) Public preview: SDK ergonomics docs + migration guide for token-only clients. (6 weeks)

Open questions / tradeoffs: 
- How heavy should schema_registry entries be? (IDs only vs. full schema inline) Recommendation: prefer IDs with optional inline schema for first-party tools.
- Should tool_call be synchronous by default? We propose asynchronous (model issues call, platform ack, later result) for scalability.
- How to surface per-frame cost to users in a way that is not confusing? We can aggregate but surface estimates in meta and finalize.

Next steps / immediate to-dos: 
- Align with serving-runtime team on feasibility of emitting non-token structured frames from current model runners (Omar).
- Spike on checkpoint retention storage cost estimate and resume semantics (Miles).
- JS + Python SDK API prototype and design doc for ToolSession (Jenna).
- Draft telemetry schema for Console and link to product telemetry backlog (create JIRA).

Notes / references: 
- This is intentionally pragmatic: we prefer a small set of frame types that cover the most common patterns over a fully general RPC.
- Keep absolute binary compatibility options open (WS frames vs SSE lines); the spec should be transport-agnostic.
